title: Artificial Aphasias in Lesioned Language Models
claim: Different components, when disrupted, yield distinct symptom mixtures, showing functional specialization hidden by similar overall error rates.
layout: 2 panels side by side; stacked bars per component, raw vs. relative to mean
description: Two side-by-side stacked bar charts share an x-axis of seven model components: Q, K, V, O, U, D and G. Panel A, 'Raw Symptom Rates', shows the mean TAB flags per response. The bars are similar in height, about 1.3 to 1.45, and each has a black 95% CI error bar. The bars are stacked from red semantic at the bottom, through green syntactic, orange fluency and blue phonological, to a large purple 'Other' block on top. Shading within each color separates the specific symptoms. Panel B, 'Relative Symptom Rates', plots each component's per-symptom contribution relative to the all-output ablated mean, centered on a zero line. Q and K sit far below zero, with large blue phonological blocks. U, D and G sit above zero. This shows large component differences that Panel A hides. A single legend for the five symptom classes runs along the bottom.
caption: Component lesions produce different TAB-symptom mixtures. (A) Raw stacked TAB-symptom rates per component, colored by symptom class and shaded by specific symptom; bars can exceed 1 because each response can receive multiple symptoms. Error bars show 95% CIs for total symptom burden. (B) Component-specific contribution, computed as each component's per-symptom rate as a multiple of the all-output ablated mean for that symptom, minus one. Values above 0 mark symptoms that are overrepresented for that component; values below 1 mark symptoms that are underrepresented.
abstract: Aphasias, selective language impairments which can arise from brain damage, reveal the functional organization of human language by providing causal links between affected brain regions and specific symptom profiles. Drawing on this literature, we introduce an aphasia-inspired technique to characterize the emergent functional organization of language models (LMs). We ``lesion'' (zero-out) model parameters and measure the effects of this intervention against clinical aphasia symptoms, as diagnosed by the Text Aphasia Battery (TAB). When applied to 112,426 outputs from five 1B-scale LMs, the full range of evaluated symptoms surface, but in distributions largely distinct from those of humans. Our method uncovers broad symptom-profile differences between attention components (query, key, value, output) and feed-forward components (up, gate, down), with weaker evidence for differences among components within the same mechanism. We also find an effect of depth, where lesions in early layers disproportionately cause syntactic and semantic symptoms while late-middle layers yield higher rates of phonological and fluency deficits. Although some LM lesions induce quantitatively more similar profiles to some human aphasia types than others, qualitative differences in symptom patterns between LMs and humans suggest that aphasia syndromes are heavily influenced by the details of learning and processing rather than being a domain-invariant consequence of disrupted language processing.
